title: LEARN Science: A K-2 Life Science and Reading Program in Public Libraries to Improve Science Achievement through Storytelling
text: Poor science achievement in childhood negatively impacts adult health, due to poor scientific literacy and reasoning. LEARN Science – Library Efforts to Advance Reading and Nutrition Science – is an informal life science and reading program through a nutrition science lens to improve science knowledge and science identity among children in kindergarten through second grade (K-2) in Mississippi using public libraries. LEARN Science leverages an opportunity for improved science achievement; improved understanding of the role of public libraries in both science and health education and promotion; and improved health of children – now and in the future – by empowering them to make food choices for chronic disease prevention through hands-on nutrition education.

title: Neural circuits mediating motivation deficits in an Alzheimer's disease rat model
text:
Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is linked to progressive cognitive function loss. Critically, neuropsychiatric symptoms
including apathy related to a loss of motivation are linked often poorer prognosis in cognitive decline. This
proposal aims to use a transgenic rat model that recapitulates AD pathology to determine the neural circuits
linked to motivated behavior and whether we can restore function via manipulating the mesolimbic dopamine
system.

title: Decoding the Ubiquitin and Autophagy Signaling Networks
text:
Dysfunctional ubiquitin and autophagy pathways are pivotal in cellular health. These pathways, crucial for cellular
homeostasis, play a significant role in the proper functioning and survival of cells. Our work focuses on
investigating the intricacies of pathways involving the ubiquitin and lysosome machinery using quantitative cell
biological and proteomics approaches.

title: Elucidating chronic liver disease pathways using somatic genetics
text:
There are no high throughput genetic methods to uncover mechanisms that drive chronic liver disease's
progression to cirrhosis, limiting our ability to develop new therapies. Recently, we showed that some somatic
mutations within diseased livers can exert adaptive effects that might benefit tissue health. Using new
technologies developed in my lab, we propose to exploit somatic mosaicism as a genetic strategy to 1) identify
adaptive genetic pathways and 2) understand how mutant clones expand within chronically damaged tissues,
and potentially protect from disease.

title: Interrogating the roles of truncated/mutated inverted terminal repeat sequences in adeno-associated virus vectors in transgene stability through episome formation and host cell genome integration
text:
This project proposal seeks to define if mutations in inverted terminal repeat (ITR) sequences, which are
the last remnants of viral elements found in adeno-associated virus (AAV)-based gene therapy vectors, can
influence the stability and safety of therapeutic transgenes. Using advanced next-generation sequencing
approaches and appropriate cell culture and animal models, this work will help to link a previously enigmatic
feature of AAV genomes to imperfections observed in vector genomes that result from potentially avoidable
manufacturing errors. The project will help to inform whether heterogeneity in ITRs are risk factors for host-cell
integration and tumorigenesis.

title: Protein-RNA interactions in cancer
text:
Cancers such as acute leukemia exploit abnormal RNA regulation and altered
metabolism to sustain their growth. This project will determine how the RNA-binding
protein IGF2BP3 links cellular metabolism to RNA modifications that control gene
expression. Understanding this connection will reveal new treatment strategies and
identify biomarkers that predict response to emerging metabolic and epitranscriptomic
therapies.

title: Autoantibodies define scleroderma subgroups with distinct relationships to cancer
text:
There is growing evidence that distinct subgroups of scleroderma patients have an increased risk
of cancer, and that unique scleroderma immune responses, alone or in combination, associate
with cancer protection. It remains unknown whether cancer drives the autoimmune response
more broadly in scleroderma, whether diversified immune responses exert potent anti-tumor
pressure, and whether cancer treatment is effective scleroderma therapy. To address these
knowledge gaps, this proposal will (i) study the value of innovative cancer and immune response
measurements in identifying patients with incident cancer diagnosis, and (ii) investigate the
relationships between malignancy, the immune response, and scleroderma disease activity in two
of the largest scleroderma cohorts in the US.

title: Role of multi-drug resistant Candida auris Hyr1 / Iff-like proteins in virulence and their potential as vaccine targets
text:
Declared an “Urgent/Critical Threat” by both CDC and WHO, Candida auris infects immunosuppressed patients
and is often untreatable due to resistance to all available antifungal drugs resulting in a high mortality rate of
approximately 60%. We propose investigating the role of C. auris cell surface proteins in virulence mechanisms
and developing novel vaccine strategies.

title: DEFINING THE ROLE OF CO-TRANSCRIPTIONAL REGULATION IN HUMAN CELL FATE TRANSITIONS
text:
Co-transcriptional RNA processing is essential for proper gene regulation, but its role in human development
remains poorly understood. This research will determine how the dual RNA/DNA binding protein ILF3 prevents
aberrant RNA editing and ensures proper splicing of developmental genes during human cell fate transitions. By
uncovering these primate-specific regulatory mechanisms, our work will identify novel therapeutic targets for
birth defects and developmental disorders where RNA processing is disrupted.

title: Determining the Origins and Vulnerabilities of Pediatric Treatment-Induced Gliomas
text:
Pediatric radiation-induced gliomas (RIG) are understudied, uniformly fatal brain cancers that arise as a
result of therapeutic cranial radiation given for other childhood cancers. We have established key
molecular features that differentiate these tumors from other pediatric high-grade gliomas, as well as a
set of novel patient-derived models. In this project, we will use these resources to advance
understanding of germline risk factors for RIG, oncogenesis, and translatable treatment strategies.

title: Using ecological momentary data to inform a web-intervention for romantic partners concerned about their loved ones drinking
text:
Concerned partners (CPs) are a powerful and often underutilized source of influence for individuals who
misuse alcohol. This project will: (1) identify specific behaviors enacted by CPs that relate to increases and
decreases in their partner’s drinking behaviors; (2) use that information to develop a web-based intervention
for CPs; and (3) evaluate the success of this intervention in reducing drinking and related problems.

title: Renal Vascular Smooth Muscle NaV Channels: Regulation and Contribution to Hypoperfusion in Neonatal Ischemic Acute Kidney Injury
text:
Acute kidney injury (AKI) in neonates is a significant public health concern, leading to long-term kidney damage
and increased mortality. This research investigates the role of voltage-gated sodium channels in regulating renal
vascular resistance and their contribution to ischemia-reperfusion-induced AKI. Understanding these
mechanisms will provide critical insights into the pathophysiology of neonatal AKI and identify new therapeutic
targets to improve outcomes in this vulnerable population.

title: Central and Peripheral Mechanisms of Corneal Pain
text:
This proposal investigates neurons that transmit information related to corneal pain and determines how they
are modified after corneal inflammation and nerve injury. Populations of corneal pain-activated neurons in the
trigeminal ganglion and brainstem are characterized based on their gene transcription profiles, and the ability
of corneal immune cells to interact and modify the properties of corneal neurons is examined. This
comprehensive analysis will provide knowledge needed to develop new treatments for corneal pain and
related disorders.

title: Applying a just-in-time adaptive intervention framework to understand and treat dynamic, symptom-maintaining stress among individuals with comorbid obesity and pain
text: PROJECT-003 Chronic pain and obesity are costly, highly comorbid, and contribute to significant personal suffering. Chronic pain is the leading cause of disability world-wide and most expensive health condition in the U.S. Over 40% of U.S. adults have obesity, which increases risk of chronic pain and worsens chronic pain outcomes. Stress early in life is a significant risk factor for obesity and pain in adulthood and daily experiences of stress are robust momentary risk factors for activating obesity-maintaining behaviors (high fat/sugar food intake, inactivity) and pain states (pain intensity, interference with daily life). Thus, stress is a unifying and modifiable risk factor for comorbid obesity and pain. There is growing evidence that stress, obesity-maintaining behaviors, and pain states, and the relationships between them are dynamic—meaning that they vary across individuals and contexts and change over time. While evidence-based treatments for obesity, pain, and stress exist, they tend to only target one of these conditions at a time and overlook the dynamic nature of each of these treatment targets. Importantly, patients report desiring integrated, personalized treatments to support them during daily life. Just- in-time adaptive interventions (JITAIs) can address these unmet needs of individuals with comorbid obesity and pain. By leveraging smart phones and wearables to monitor individuals in daily life, the right type and amount of evidence-based support can be delivered in real time when people need it. To leverage the JITAI approach for targeting stress among those with comorbid obesity and pain, the critical first step is to identify which features and under what circumstances stress moves an individual into a period of high risk for experiencing pain symp- toms and/or engaging in obesity-maintaining behaviors. This information guides other key features of the inter- vention---who needs intervention, when do they need it, and what type of intervention will best meet their needs in the moment. The goal of this Phase 2 STAR COBRE Research Project is to conduct formative intensive longitudinal data collection to guide design of a novel JITAI targeting stress to reduce obesity-maintaining be- haviors and pain states. First, a community advisory board of adults with comorbid obesity/pain will be estab- lished to provide input on all aspects of the following research procedures. We will then recruit n=78 adults with obesity and pain to complete assessments at baseline and at 12-wks (including 7 days of ecological momentary assessment and actigraphy, REDCap surveys, and anthropometrics). Multilevel modeling will be used to identify which features of stress and context are the strongest predictors of obesity-maintaining behaviors and pain states. A repository of evidence-based strategies will be developed based on these predictors and translated into a format for momentary/digital delivery. By completion a blueprint of the JITAI and supporting technology will be finalized. This will position the new and early-stage investigator Dr. KayLoni Olson, PhD, to pursue R01-level funding for a micro-randomized trial testing the efficacy of the JITAI to address comorbidity of obesity and pain by targeting the critical role of stress processes in propagating poor health across the lifespan.

title: Chemical toolbox for multiscale, integrative imaging: Connecting cellular gene expression to organ-scale phenotype
text:
One of the core questions in biology is how the genetic alteration in a cell translates into organ-level
phenotype, especially for the phenotypes affecting human health. We propose to develop a multiscale,
integrative imaging platform that probes organ-scale phenotype, subcellular phenotype, and single-cell genotype
in the same tissue by innovating appropriate chemical and imaging tools. The new platform will help researchers
identify the molecular basis of structural and functional abnormalities in diseased tissues and study how a focal
point of abnormality affects nearby cells and propagates.

title: Targeted delivery of nanomedicines to the coronary microvasculature during ex vivo normothermic perfusion of marginal human hearts
text:
We present here a novel approach for targeted delivery of nanomedicines to the coronary microvasculature
during ex vivo normothermic perfusion of marginal human hearts. Our approach is based on powerful new
methods for nanoparticle targeting and incorporates advanced diagnostic imaging tools to characterize
nanoparticle accumulation as well as myocardial perfusion and function. The goal of this work is to develop
targeted therapies to treat ischemia-reperfusion injury and improve the availability hearts for transplantation

title: Mitigation of gastrointestinal acute radiation syndrome by promoting clusterin-mediated intestinal regeneration
text:
Radiation tolerance of the gastrointestinal (GI) tract can be exceeded in radiation accidents at nuclear power
plants or after the detonation of a nuclear weapon or radioactive bomb, resulting in a lethal GI acute radiation
syndrome (GI-ARS). The overall goal of this project is to define novel mechanisms by which Clusterin
promotes the regeneration of the intestinal epithelium in response to severe radiation injury in mouse and
human intestinal organoids, and to build upon this knowledge to develop novel mitigators for GI-ARS.

title: Surface-Based Fiber Tracking and Modeling Techniques for Mapping the Superficial White Matter Connectome with Diffusion MRI
text:
Relevance to Public Health
Our project will provide fundamentally novel solutions to map the superficial white matter connectome by
developing surface-based tools for fiber tracking, atlas construction, personalized analysis, and personalized
tools for data harmonization. These novel tools will allow brain imaging researchers to augment their current
connectome models with U-fibers in superficial white matter and more completely map human brain
connectomes in various brain disorders.

title: Contributions of Self-Focused Attention to Early Warning Indicators of CBT Non-Response
text:
Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is the most effective psychological treatment for anxiety and obsessive
compulsive related disorders, yet approximately half of patients with these disorders who receive CBT fail to
achieve sustained clinical remission. No reliable biomarker of CBT non-response exists. This study will
determine whether early changes in a specific biomarker, self-focused attention, will represent a sensitive
predictor and potential mechanism of CBT non-response.

title: Probes, Inhibitors, and PROTACs (PIP) Core
text: Probes, Inhibitors, and PROTACs (PIP) Core The overarching mission of the PIP Core is to use sophisticated chemistry and mass spectrometry for development of small molecules that facilitate molecular target discovery and development. Genetic methods are routinely used to identify, develop, and validate molecular targets. These methods rely on altering the DNA or RNA sequences of the protein target. However, drug discovery relies on manipulating the function of the corresponding proteins using small molecules. Often the results obtained through these complementary strategies do not correlate.1 The incongruence associated with the results from these orthogonal approaches can be attributed to the complex biology that is dependent on multiple functions i.e., enzymatic and scaffolding, associated with the protein target. Modulating protein levels by altering the nucleic acids eliminates all the target protein functions. However small molecule modulators can be tuned to induce either domain specific effects (reversible or irreversible) or removal of the entire protein (PROTAC) with exquisite temporal control. These could be tagged with photoactivatable or fluorescent molecules, or biotin to enable target identification and validation, study mechanism of action, or characterize the associated interactome. In addition to the design and synthesis of above types of small molecules, the PIP Core will also provide scale up services (mg to g) for additional experiments such as in vivo validation of targets and hit-to-lead optimization studies to generate structure activity relationship (SAR) data. Mass spectrometry will be used to characterize the impact of these compounds on the proteome through quantitative analysis of proteins and posttranslational or chemical modifications to validate mechanism of action and compensatory features that may contribute to drug resistance. The Core will be led by Drs. Natarajan and Woods, who will bring complementary expertise to the PIP Core. Dr. Natarajan has extensive expertise in developing probes, inhibitors, and PROTACs, using cutting edge chemistry methods. Dr. Woods has extensive experience using mass spectrometry as a platform for delineating protein- protein interactions, posttranslational modifications, and multivariate biomarkers of cancer response to therapy. PIP Core services will be extensively utilized by CMTDD Research Project Leaders (RPLs), CMTDD members and University researchers at large.
